title: Joseph the Dreamer Sold by His Brothers
summary: Jacob loves Joseph more than his other sons and gives him a special robe, and Joseph's dreams of his family bowing to him deepen his brothers' hatred. When Jacob sends him to check on them, they strip him, throw him into a dry cistern, and sell him to traders bound for Egypt. They deceive their father with the robe dipped in goat's blood, Jacob mourns and refuses comfort, and Joseph is sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh.
story: With Isaac buried (35:29) and Esau's line recorded (chapter 36), Genesis opens its last major section: “This is the account of Jacob” (verse 2). It runs to the end of the book, and though it bears Jacob's name, its main character is Joseph, with Judah close behind. The chapter plants every seed of the story to come. The favoritism that divided Isaac's household and Jacob's marriages now falls on the next generation, the brothers' hatred turns murderous, and the dreams that seem to die in the pit will come true in Egypt when the brothers bow before a governor they don't recognize (42:6). Genesis is also moving the family toward Egypt, where Exodus will find them. The chapter ends with Jacob refusing all comfort and Joseph sold as a slave, and God isn't mentioned once. Readers are left to learn, as the brothers eventually do, that he was never absent (45:5-8; 50:20).
historical:
The Joseph story is set in Egypt, and its date is debated. On the Bible's own chronology, reckoned back from 1 Kings 6:1, Joseph's career would fall around the nineteenth century BC, during Egypt's Middle Kingdom. Many scholars link it instead with the Hyksos period (about 1650-1550 BC), when rulers of West Semitic origin controlled northern Egypt, which would make a foreigner's rise to high office easier to explain. Others regard the story as a later composition that draws its Egyptian color from the first millennium BC. What is certain is that people from Canaan and Syria went down to Egypt throughout this era as traders, as herders seeking food, and as slaves. A painting in a tomb at Beni Hasan from about 1900 BC shows a group of Asiatics in brightly patterned clothing arriving in Egypt, and an Egyptian papyrus from the eighteenth century BC lists household servants with Semitic names.

The route in the chapter is realistic. Dothan, about fifteen miles north of Shechem, lay near a pass where traffic from Gilead, east of the Jordan, crossed the hills toward the coastal road to Egypt. The caravan carries goods Gilead was known for, including the balm Jeremiah later mentions (Jeremiah 8:22), resins and aromatics prized in Egypt for medicine, perfume, and embalming. Twenty shekels of silver was a plausible price for a young man; Israel's law later valued a male between five and twenty at exactly that sum (Leviticus 27:5).
cultural:
Jacob's gift to Joseph was more than a garment. The Hebrew phrase rendered robe of many colors is uncertain; it may describe a robe with long sleeves or one richly ornamented, but either way it was not work clothing. The only other place the phrase appears is 2 Samuel 13:18, for the robe worn by the king's virgin daughters. For a younger son to wear it while his older brothers tended flocks signaled honor and perhaps the firstborn's standing, which Reuben had forfeited (35:22; 1 Chronicles 5:1-2). Dreams were taken seriously in the ancient world as messages from the divine realm, and Egyptians kept written guides to interpreting them. A dream given twice, the second repeating the first in a new image, was especially certain, a principle Joseph himself states later (41:32).

The pit was a cistern, a bottle-shaped hole cut into rock to store winter rain, narrow at the mouth and impossible to climb out of, and an empty one made a ready prison, as Jeremiah later found (Jeremiah 38:6). The brothers' lie relied on a real danger, since shepherds lost animals, and sometimes their lives, to lions and bears. Jacob's mourning follows custom: tearing his clothes, wearing sackcloth (rough cloth of goat hair), and refusing to be comforted. His words about going down to Sheol mourning mean he expects to grieve until he dies.
literary: The chapter is driven by seeing, speaking, and recognizing. The brothers see their father's love and cannot speak a kind word to Joseph (verse 4); they see him from a distance and plot (verse 18); they mock him as that dreamer (verse 19). The robe frames the plot: given in love (verse 3), stripped off in hate (verse 23), dipped in blood and sent home (verses 31-32). The deception mirrors Jacob's own past. He once fooled his father with goat skins and his brother's clothes (27:9, 15-16); now his sons fool him with a goat's blood and his son's robe. Their words, “Examine it to see whether it is your son's robe or not” (verse 32), use a verb, recognize, that echoes through the next chapters, when Judah is asked to recognize his own seal (38:25) and when Joseph recognizes his brothers while they fail to recognize him (42:7-8). Reuben and Judah emerge as two kinds of leader: Reuben means well but fails, and Judah, though he proposes a sale, takes charge. The father's rebuke of the second dream, which pictures Joseph's mother bowing though Rachel has died (35:19), shows dream imagery at work, the whole family pictured as sun, moon, and stars, rather than a literal forecast.

outline.t: Jacob's favoritism and the brothers' hatred
Joseph sent to find his brothers
The bloodied robe and Jacob's grief
Joseph sold to Potiphar in Egypt

doctrines.note: God is never named here, yet this chapter begins the clearest picture of providence in Genesis. Every human choice in it is sinful or foolish (a father's favoritism, a son's tactlessness, brothers' hatred, a cruel lie), and God will weave all of it into the rescue of the family. Joseph's later words interpret the chapter: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (50:20).

Envy grows by stages: resentment of a father's love, hatred, the inability to speak kindly, a plot to kill, and finally a lie told to a grieving father while the liars pretend to comfort him. The chapter is a case study in how unchecked resentment becomes cruelty.

Jacob repeats his parents' mistake. Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob (25:28), and now Jacob openly loves one son more than the rest. The chapter shows what favoritism does both to those passed over and to the favored child.

words.note: Ketonet, tunic or robe, the long garment worn over the body. It is the word for the garments God made for Adam and Eve (3:21) and for the tunics of Israel's priests (Exodus 28:4). Joseph's is described with the rare word passim, which may mean long-sleeved or ornamented. The robe is mentioned eight times in the chapter, and the plot can be traced by what happens to it.

Nakar, to recognize or examine closely. The brothers ask their father to recognize the robe (verse 32), and he does (verse 33), drawing exactly the false conclusion they intended. The verb returns when Tamar asks Judah to recognize his seal and staff (38:25-26) and when Joseph recognizes his brothers in Egypt (42:7-8). Recognition, false and true, is one of the threads that binds Joseph's story together.

Sheol, the realm of the dead, appears here for the first time in the Bible (verse 35). The Old Testament often pictures it as a shadowy place below the earth where the dead go down. Jacob means he will carry his grief to the grave. The Old Testament says little about Sheol, and later Scripture brings a fuller hope of resurrection (Daniel 12:2).

christ: The New Testament reads Joseph's story as a pattern that Jesus fulfills, and this chapter supplies much of it. Stephen, preaching before the council in Jerusalem, said, “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him” (Acts 7:9), setting Joseph beside Jesus as a deliverer first rejected by his own people. Joseph is the beloved son, sent by his father to his brothers, hated, plotted against, stripped of his garment, and sold for silver. Jesus told a parable of a vineyard owner who finally sent his son to the tenants, who said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance” (Matthew 21:38), words that recall the brothers' “Come now, let us kill him” (verse 20). The Gospels record Jesus betrayed for silver and stripped of his clothing before his crucifixion. None of this makes Genesis 37 a prediction; Joseph is a real man with real faults. But the pattern of a beloved son rejected by his own and raised up to save them is the pattern of the gospel.

hard.q: Who sold Joseph: the brothers, the Ishmaelites, or the Midianites?
hard.a:
The chapter names both Ishmaelites (verses 25, 27, 28) and Midianites (verses 28, 36) as the traders, and verse 28 can be read in more than one way. In one reading, the brothers pulled Joseph out and sold him to the Ishmaelites, and the Midianites in the same verse are the same traders under another name. Judges 8:24 supports this, since it describes Midianites as Ishmaelites, apparently using Ishmaelite as a general term for caravan traders from the desert. In another reading, Midianite traders passed by and pulled Joseph out of the pit themselves while the brothers were eating, then sold him to the Ishmaelites, which would explain Reuben's shock at finding the pit empty (verse 29). Many scholars see instead two versions of the story, one with Ishmaelites and one with Midianites, woven together by a later editor.

Whatever the mechanics, the Bible holds the brothers responsible. Judah proposed the sale (verses 26-27), and years later Joseph tells them plainly, “I am Joseph, your brother” who was “sold into Egypt” (45:4), and they don't deny it. The brothers' guilt, not the identity of the traders, is what the rest of the story works through.

questions: Jacob's favoritism was obvious to all his sons. Where have you seen favoritism, at home or elsewhere, produce the kind of resentment this chapter describes?
Joseph's brothers could not speak a kind word to him, and their hatred grew until they could imagine killing him. How does envy grow when it is left unchecked?
God isn't mentioned in this chapter, yet the whole Joseph story shows him at work in it. How might that change the way you read seasons when God seems absent?
